$comment: Mutations as CONCRETE PATCHES, per §4.1c of the catalog's _MASTER-TEMPLATE.md.
A sentence describing a mutation cannot be replayed, and a paragraph describing
a run is the author's side of the claim rather than the run's. So each entry
below is a list of patches, and each patch names a file, an anchor that must
occur EXACTLY ONCE in it, and the text that replaces it. `npm run mutations`
applies them one mutation at a time and writes LEDGER.json and LEDGER.md
itself; no `observed` value in either file is typed by a person.
The five entries are the three the build brief names - a decryption that always
returns the plaintext, a verification that always accepts, and the wrong-key
path silently reusing the right key - plus the two §4.1d requires of any
negative claim: delete the claim text and the assertion that it is on screen
must fail; break a check inside the fixture and the assertion that everything
Every patch is chosen to COMPILE. A patch that does not build is recorded as
DOES NOT BUILD and is never a kill, because the suite would then run against
the last good bundle and pass having proved nothing.

mutations.what: `open()` ignores the key it is handed and returns whatever `close()` last locked, so any private key appears to open the lock.
mutations.why: This is the mutation a round-trip test cannot see, which is why the brief names it. Encrypt-then-decrypt still returns the message; Step 3's OPENED verdict is unchanged; the claims test that checks the recovered note still passes. What breaks is the REFUSAL, which is the only thing a lock actually promises. The unit suite's cross-pair rejection catches it too, and that redundancy is deliberate - the browser verdict and the algorithmic test are two independent witnesses to the same property.

patches.anchor: /** Why a message cannot be locked, in the reader's words. Null means it can. */

mutations.owningTest: Step 3 wrong key is refused CALMLY, and the page names the cause
mutations.expectOnPage: OPENED WITH THE WRONG KEY, in the alarm tone - the one state on this page that earns an alarm, because something that had to fail did not.

mutations.what: `check()` runs the real verification and then discards its answer, returning true.
mutations.why: Every signing round-trip stays green - a real signature still verifies - and so does Step 4's VERIFIED verdict. What breaks is the tamper path: one character changed and the check accepts it anyway. The page is built to paint that as an alarm rather than a pass, so the mutation is visible in the verdict tone as well as in the headline.

mutations.expectOnPage: VERIFIED THE TAMPERED TEXT, in the alarm tone.

mutations.what: Step 3's wrong-key button generates a second pair, prints its genuinely different fingerprint, and then opens the lock with the READER'S OWN private half.
mutations.why: The subtlest of the three and the one a careless implementation really produces, because nothing about it looks wrong: a fresh pair IS generated, so the two fingerprints on screen genuinely differ and the panel reads exactly as intended. Only the key handed to `open` is the wrong one. Every unit test stays green - this is a UI wiring defect, not a cryptographic one - so the browser verdict is the only witness.

mutations.what: The negative-claim sentence is emptied, so the fixture renders with no statement of the limitation it exists to demonstrate.
mutations.why: §4.1d requires exactly this check: delete the negative-claim text and the assertion that it is on screen must fail. Note what does NOT break - the fixture still reaches its state, every verdict is still green, and the verdict still reads OPENED - AND UNATTRIBUTED - so nothing but the claim assertion can catch it. A negative-claim test that survives its own text being deleted is decorative.
mutations.owningTest: every check passes, and the message is unattributed anyway
mutations.expectOnPage: The fixture state exactly as it ships, minus the one sentence that makes it a result rather than a curiosity.

mutations.what: The stranger's block is opened with a freshly generated private half instead of the reader's, so the fixture's own decryption fails.
mutations.why: The other half of what §4.1d requires: break a check inside the fixture and the assertion that everything is green must fail. The page then renders THE FIXTURE DID NOT HOLD, which is the honest outcome - a fixture whose own checks fail is demonstrating the mechanism working rather than its limit, and must never be allowed to read as a demonstration of the limitation.
